newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. signals tacit support for Colombia candidate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. signals tacit support for Colombia candidate.

text.p: The U.S. envoy to Colombia signalled Washington's tacit support on Friday for Alfonso Valdivieso, the respected corruption fighter who resigned as chief prosecutor on Thursday and announced his candidacy for Colombia's presidency.
"We've lost a person I've worked very closely with," Ambassador Myles Frechette told reporters, when asked about Valdivieso's decision to step down as prosecutor-general.
"My government, the Justice Department, has worked very closely with the prosecutor-general's office," Frechette said, adding: "I wish him the best of luck."

Valdivieso, who polls consistently show to be Colombia's most popular and respected public figure, was appointed in 1994, shortly after President Ernesto Samper took office amid a scandal over charges that he used drug money to finance his election campaign.
Valdivieso made his mark, and won many allies in Washington, by spearheading an independent probe into the finance scandal that nearly toppled Samper on drug-corruption charges last year.

Frechette answered with a curt "of course" when asked if Washington had lost a friend in the prosecutor-general's office but now stood to gain one in the ornate Casa de Narino presidential palace next year.

Political analysts and diplomats say Valdivieso's strongest challenger in his bid for Colombia's top job is Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, who is likely to step down within a matter of weeks to launch his own candidacy.
Serpa, a firebrand populist and Samper's right-hand man, has had frequent run-ins with the United States over drug policy and U.S. allegations of high-level government corruption in Colombia.
The elections will be held in May next year and Colombian law requires that anyone in public office intending to run for the country's top job step down a year ahead of the polls.
